title: Tuxedo band 1927 record and the 1930 Buena Vista season in Biloxi
summary: Frazier recalls being chosen as drummer for a record, then lists the Tuxedo band members on the 1930 summer job in Biloxi and the weekend drives home.

story.theme_name: Who was in the band: naming sidemen and personnel
story.community_name: Who played in the band: reciting personnel

blocks.x: That was the Young Morgan Band. Well, they called it Sam Morgan Band. Sam Morgan Band. Sam Morgan Band. But, say, Sammy got the best go year. You know, Johnny Day, I picked him right now, standing on Seminole in Claiborne waiting to catch the North Claiborne called the Ride Up Canal Street. Yeah. Well, that same year you're speaking about was John Morrell had got several fellas out there in the tuxedo band to make that record. I see. And he had wanted, Chani Bebe was the drummer, you see, but he was a crack drummer. But they wanted me to play on the con and they figured Chani might get high or something and blow him up. Not for better playing, but this figure that, this like in 1930 when I went over to Biloxo with Tuxedo Band, they played at a seasoned job at the Buena Vista Hotel. And see they had what they called stop time. And then for the Gitter Man, so I was playing with the Piran Band during them days, and they asked me to play that's a seasoned job. It starts in, it ends up on a Labor Day, but it starts in I think in the middle part of July. It's supposed to be ten weeks or something like that. Yeah. Well we used to play from, how that was, from eleven to twelve in the day called Breakfast Dance. It's still running? Yeah. And then we played from five to six, and then we'd come back and go play from nine to twelve. Monday's True Sadness, and you had the Mississippi Blue Law, we'd come home on a Sunday with those who want to come home. That was where I bring it back in 1930 now. That's when I played that season with the Tuxedo Band. I'll give you the members of that band. Yeah, yeah. Well that band at that time consisted of, first had Bill Matthew on trombone, and Papa Celeste on cornet, and Rick High Lexie on cornet, two cornets. And the sax session consisted of a boy by the name of Sun Johnson, he's on this picture here now, he was good, and we had Joe Ruzon, he's out in L.A. right now on sax, another good man, and we had this boy, Edmund Hall, that's the other one, Clarence Hall on tenor sax.
So Paul Barch wasn't doing that band anymore then? Who? Paul Barch was gone. Oh no, no. He was up in New York that time.

Paul Barch wouldn't play in the band that time, got to play in 1930. And then during that time when Joe Ruzon got hoisted, had like a B or something, he kind of hoisted his mouth, so we replaced him with this fellow Caesar Thornton. Yeah, yeah. Yeah, he's from St. Louis, and he came down here on the boat. Not too much with sax, but he was a good arranger. They had him play with the band, he finished it there, and then he started arranging for the band while he was on the seasoned job. And then come down, and Jeanette was, I mean, Mercedes Gorman was playing the piano in Jeanette Sullivan's place, because he was expecting a first child.

You see, that's Marvin Kimmel's wife. Right. Jeanette's, well we called her Sullivan, but I don't think she, yeah she married to Kimmel then, that's right. So I used to bring money for him, for Kimmel to help people, that girl came from, from, uh, uh, Patschristian, Mississippi. Mm-hmm. And every Sunday, Kimmel had a Buick Roast call, and I had a force on the Dodge call, well I used to drive home every Sunday, and go back on a Monday morning, well I used to ride Caesar, that's all the sax section, and sometimes Rick, he's still over the lake too, because he's from the Bay St. Louis, you see. Yeah. And that's his little brother playing the drum right now by the Mason Boybin.

Yeah. And Lester. Yeah, Little Lester, and them boys was all small in there. Yeah, that was the group. I was on the drum, yeah. Mm-hmm. That was the band. So Merced Deez was playing in Jeanette Sullivan's place. I see. Yeah, with that band, dude. That was 1930.
